articles.title: MSME Ministry Holds Round Table on SC/ST MSE Procurement
articles.description: A Round Table Discussion with Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) was held on 5 November 2026 at Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, New Delhi to monitor procurement status of CPSEs on mandated 4% from SC/ST MSEs under Public Procurement Policy of Government. Ms. Mercy Epao, Joint Secretary, Ministry of MSME chaired the meeting. Shri Ajit Chavan, Additional Chief Executive Officer, GeM, Dr. S.S Acharya, Chairman-cum-Managing Director, NSIC and other Senior Officers from Ministry, Department of Public Enterprises and NSIC participated and share their respective interventions to support the SC/ST MSEs. A total of 30 CPSEs including BHEL, BEL, NTPC, AAI, BEML, Coal India Ltd participated in the Round Table discussion, which centred on the challenges being faced by the CPSEs and sharing of best practices and how to deepen coordination between NSSHOs, GeM and CPSEs. In her address, Ms. Mercy Epao, highlighted various initiatives undertaken to promote and handhold to SC/ST MSEs under National SC-ST Hub (NSSH) Scheme. This resulted in continuous increase in the share of SC/ST MSEs in public procurement. In FY 2025-26, more than 36 times hike in public procurement from SC/ST MSE since inception of the scheme. She further informed about Entrepreneur Awareness & Special Vendor Development Program (EA&SVDP), a new initiative for creation of awareness amongst SC/ST MSE and to network with CPSEs. She urged CPSEs to formulate internal action plan to achieve the target and also provide support in terms of Vendor Registration/Enlistment Procedure, Product/Service Matchmaking, Regional/Local Connect of CPSEs with SC/ST MSEs and Handholding support. Shri Ajit Chavan, Additional CEO, GeM, acknowledged the Ministry of MSME’s significant contribution towards empowering small enterprises and achieving key milestones under the public procurement framework. He informed about various measures taken to facilitate SC/ST MSEs in tender participation including identification of SC/ST MSE sellers through dedicated marketplace filters. He emphasized the importance of engaging sellers from diverse sectors, particularly on services and industry verticals to ensure equitable access to procurement opportunities. He encouraged CPSEs to utilize the services of the Nodal Officer appointed by GeM for handholding support. The Round Table provided an opportunity for CPSEs to interact with best performing CPSEs, to address their gaps/challenges. The discussion also focused on identifying avenues for enhanced collaboration between CPSEs and NSSH through vendor development programs, capacity-building initiatives and digital facilitation support to strengthen procurement from SC/ST and women-owned MSEs.

articles.title: Shakti Pumps: PM-KUSUM 2.0 Holds the Key to Investor Cheer, but the Solar Pump Industry Faces a Turf War
articles.description: Readinjg through the transcript of the Shakt Pumps analyst call after its Q2 results, it is clear that the immediate hope is that PM-KUSUM 2.0 will revive the momentum that made solar pumps one of India's more attractive clean-energy manufacturing opportunities. But the wait for the scheme is exposing a larger problem for the sector: a business built around government-backed procurement is now searching for its next growth engine, even as competition intensifies from both established players and new entrants. Shakti installed 23,865 solar pumps in Q2 FY27, around 7% more than a year earlier, generating solar EPC revenue of approximately Rs 543 crore. Yet the company's management acknowledged that pricing flexibility remains limited, with business concentrated around a small number of active tenders, particularly Maharashtra's Magel Tyala scheme. The company is looking to PM-KUSUM 2.0 for a fresh pipeline. Management expected the scheme to receive approval during the ongoing quarter, with execution benefits following in the next quarter. But it also acknowledged that the timing remains in the government's hands, with the scheme undergoing revisions. The expectation, therefore, is not the same as an assured order pipeline. The pressure is visible in margins. Raw material costs rose around 3% sequentially, while internal cost optimisation helped offset much of the increase. But management was unwilling to offer a firm margin outlook until the new scheme's pricing and tender rates become clearer. The company's order book of around Rs 750 crore offers near-term execution visibility, but not necessarily a durable answer to the pricing problem. The diversification scramble The more consequential development is that all three listed companies associated with India's solar pump business—Shakti Pumps, GK Energy and Oswal Pumps—have moved into rooftop solar. The logic is understandable: they already have relationships with customers, installation networks and experience in deploying solar systems. Rooftop offers an opportunity to use some of that infrastructure to build a business beyond agricultural pump tenders. But diversification does not automatically mean better profitability. Rooftop solar is a competitive EPC market, with customer acquisition, installation costs, financing, service obligations and price competition all affecting returns. The scale of the opportunity is substantial, but the margins that these companies can sustainably earn from it remain to be demonstrated. Shakti's own call illustrates the early-stage nature of the opportunity. Its rooftop revenue grew 58% year-on-year in Q2, but management said the business was still relatively small. The company expects its 500 MW module facility to help it offer a more complete rooftop solution and gradually replace externally sourced panels. Its larger 2.2 GW cell facility is planned for FY28. GK Energy has also positioned rooftop as a natural extension of its solar pump execution network, while Oswal has been expanding into residential rooftop and other solar verticals. The common thread is a search for revenue streams that are less dependent on the timing of agricultural procurement programmes. The threat is coming from the other direction While pump companies are moving into rooftop, established solar module manufacturers are entering the pump market. Saatvik Green Energy, for instance, has secured a solar water-pumping order from MSEDCL, while Insolation Energy is among the module manufacturers expanding into the solar pump opportunity. This creates a strategic dilemma for the established pump players. Should they defend their core market, where they have manufacturing experience, distribution relationships and an established position in government tenders? Or should they expand into adjacent businesses, even if that means entering segments with different competitors and uncertain returns? The reverse challenge applies to module manufacturers. Solar pumps offer a route to diversify beyond the increasingly crowded module market, but they also require capabilities in pumps, motors, controllers, installation and after-sales service. Manufacturing a module is not the same as delivering and maintaining a functioning irrigation system. The result could be a more competitive market, but not necessarily a more profitable one for any of the participants. Is backward integration arriving too late? Shakti's investment in module and cell manufacturing raises another question. The company hopes that in-house modules will improve cost control, support its rooftop business and create additional opportunities with export customers. Management has also indicated that backward integration could eventually improve margins. That logic makes sense if captive demand is large enough and the cost advantage is sustained. But the timing matters. India's module manufacturing capacity has already expanded far ahead of demand. Estimates place module capacity at approximately 233 GW as of June 2026, with factories operating at only 35–40% utilisation. The imbalance between module capacity and domestic cell capacity is also narrowing, albeit much more slowly, but expected to be a much more comfortable situation by March 2027. The risk is that by the time Shakti's larger cell facility becomes operational, the scarcity premium currently enjoyed by domestic cell capacity may have narrowed. More capacity, stronger competition and changing technology requirements could limit the margin advantage of integration. Backward integration may still offer supply security and strategic control, but it should not automatically be treated as a future margin windfall. For Shakti, the immediate priority remains improving profitability in its existing business and converting its order book into cash. PM-KUSUM 2.0 could provide the next volume trigger. But the longer-term test is whether the company can build businesses that do not depend on one government programme, without simply exchanging one low-margin competitive market for another. That is the dilemma facing India's solar pump industry. The companies are trying to protect their turf and expand it at the same time. In a market where everyone is diversifying and new competitors are arriving, growth may be easier to find than profitable growth. As Oswal Pumps announces its own results today, we will know if the promise holds.
